query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-temperature high-entropy alloys, the formation and retention of a protective oxide layer is controlled by the interplay between sluggish diffusion and the selective surface segregation of reactive elements (e.g., Cr or Al). This mechanism promotes the rapid formation of a dense, adherent oxide (such as CrTaO4 or Al2O3) that retards further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, well-homogenized high-entropy alloy with a random distribution of alloying elements including sufficient reactive components like Cr and/or Al.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples—with normal reactive element content and with reduced reactive element content or pre-treatments that modify diffusion rates—to high-temperature oxidation conditions.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (around 1000–1100°C) in controlled oxygen partial pressure environments over extended durations (e.g., up to 200 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The inherent sluggish diffusion in multicomponent HEAs promotes limited outward cation transport and controlled oxygen ingress, while preferential surface segregation of reactive elements facilitates the formation of a uniform, passivating oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature conditions, the decreased diffusivity inherent to the HEA’s disordered lattice limits both the oxidation and metal cation mobility. This, combined with the tendency of reactive elements (e.g., Cr or Al) to segregate to the surface, results in the selective formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer that acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with adequate reactive elements and inherently sluggish diffusion will form a thin, continuous, and stable oxide layer that significantly reduces further oxidation (lower weight gain and thinner scale) compared to alloys lacking these characteristics.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys or HEA samples modified to reduce reactive element content or increase diffusion kinetics, which are expected to form less protective, more porous or rapidly growing oxide scales under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under high-temperature oxidation regimes (approximately 1000–1100°C) and assumes the presence of sufficient reactive elements; extreme oxidative environments or compositions without these critical elements may not follow the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contributions of individual elements’ diffusion and segregation rates remain to be fully elucidated, leaving some uncertainty regarding the relative impact of each element and possible interactions in multi-oxide scale formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one with standard reactive element levels and inherent sluggish diffusion, and a second modified set with either lower reactive element content or a pretreatment that increases diffusion (e.g., an annealing process that reduces sluggishity). Expose both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 1100°C for 200 hours).
measurements: Oxide layer morphology and continuity (via SEM/TEM)
Oxide scale thickness and weight gain (using thermogravimetric analysis)
Surface chemistry and elemental distribution (using XPS or EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy (with reduced reactive element content or enhanced diffusion) forms an oxide layer that is as dense, continuous, and protective as the control sample—showing similar oxidation resistance—then the hypothesis that sluggish diffusion and selective surface segregation of reactive elements govern protective oxide formation is falsified.

Initial Oxidation Behavior of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Coating Produced by Atmospheric Plasma Spraying in the Range of 650 °C to 1000 °C

Abstract: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide

Abstract: AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours.
